Control the jump-off of any model

Source: R/model-anchor.R
anchored.Rd

Forecasts of most models start from their fitted rates in the last observed year. Where the fit misses the level of the last years (for example after a recent change of trend), the forecast starts with a step away from the observations; where the observations are noisy, starting from them carries the noise into every forecast year. anchored() wraps any model specification and moves the start of its forecasts towards the observed level, per age and stratum:

Usage

anchored(
  spec,
  to = c("observed", "smoothed"),
  years = 3,
  decay = 10,
  shrink = TRUE
)

Arguments

spec

A model specification.

to

"observed" or "smoothed".

years

Number of last training years whose deaths define the offset.

decay

Years over which the offset fades out (Inf: constant).

shrink

Shrink offsets of cells with few deaths.

Value

A model specification. The fitted object has the offsets in $anchor$offset ([age, stratum], log scale).

Details

  1. the offset is the log ratio of observed to fitted deaths, summed over the last years training years (to = "observed": the rates before smoothing; to = "smoothed": the rates after preprocessing, which differs when the pipeline smooths);

  2. offsets of cells with few deaths are shrunk towards the deaths-weighted mean offset of their stratum (empirical Bayes, with the Poisson variance of each offset; shrink = TRUE);

  3. the forecast draws are multiplied by exp(offset * w(h)), where the weight w(h) falls linearly from 1 at the first forecast year to 0 after decay years (decay = Inf keeps the offset, decay = 0 leaves the model's own jump-off).

With the default decay = 10, forecasts more than ten years ahead are those of the model itself; during the fade the offsets add a small apparent trend. years = 1, decay = Inf, shrink = FALSE is the observed jump-off of Lee-Carter models (lee_carter(jump_off = "observed")). Models that have no fitted rates (random walks, time series per age) start from the observed rates already and are left unchanged; in an ensemble() each draw is anchored with the offset of the component it comes from. For reconciled() models the bottom strata are anchored and the aggregates recomputed, so the draws stay coherent. mt_jump_off() reports the step between the last observed or fitted year and the first forecast year.

Anchoring helps where the fitted rates of the last year are far from the observed level. With large counts the last observed year is a good anchor; where the last observed rates are noisy, several years are better. Where the model's own jump-off is already close to the observed level, anchoring changes little and can narrow the intervals of the first years too much. The vignette "Where a forecast starts: the jump-off" shows the effect in a backtest.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2019)
fit <- mt_fit(anchored(lee_carter(), years = 3, decay = 10), x)
summary(as.vector(fit$anchor$offset))
#>       Min.    1st Qu.     Median       Mean    3rd Qu.       Max. 
#> -0.0002439 -0.0002439  0.0003177  0.0003177  0.0008793  0.0008793 
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
mt_jump_off(fc)
#>       sex  label observed   fitted forecast step_observed step_fitted
#>    <char> <char>    <num>    <num>    <num>         <num>       <num>
#> 1: female female 55.95597 55.95828 56.05399    0.09802129  0.09571211
#> 2:   male   male 51.16230 51.17137 51.26540    0.10310001  0.09403114
